title: Genomic pathogenic alterations in the SWI/SNF complex compromise the outcomes of immunotherapy in Chinese patients with KRAS-mutant NSCLC by downregulating STING expression
author: Lingling Gao; Jie Jiang; Linlin Zhu; Zhi Xie; Yu Chen; Zhiyi Lv; Yuqing Chen; Wenbin Zhou; Ji Chen; Yumin Zhong; Li Zhang; Penghui Zeng; Xiaodan Huang; Wenqing Yan; Danxia Lu; Shuilian Zhang; Weibang Guo; Dongkun Zhang; Haiyu Zhou; Weineng Feng; Binchao Wang; Zunfu Ke; Xuening Yang; Hongling Liang; Xuchao Zhang
text:
Abstract
Background
Switch/sucrose nonfermentable (SWI/SNF) complex mutations have been reported in Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homologue (KRAS)-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but the influence on immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) outcomes is debated and needs to be investigated further.
Methods
Genomic pathogenic alterations (GPAs) in SWI/SNF genes were identified via OncoKB, COSMIC and PolyPhen-2. NSCLC patients (NSCLCs) were classified according to alterations in six SWI/SNF genes (ARID1A, ARID1B, ARID2, PBRM1, SMARCA4 and SMARCB1). Cell lines used for differentially expressed gene analyses were subjected to RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) and Western blotting to validate protein expression levels. Protein expression in tumour specimens was detected by immunohistochemistry (IHC).
Results
In 2660 NSCLCs, 15.0% (401/2660) had SWI/SNF GPAs. A total of 23.1% (69/299) of the EGFRwtALKwt NSCLCs and 27.8% (25/90) of the STK11wtKEAP1wtKRASmut NSCLCs who received ICB had SWI/SNF GPAs. Among all the ICB-treated NSCLCs, progression-free survival (PFS) was not significantly different between SWI/SNF-wild type (wt) and SWI/SNF-mutant (mut) NSCLCs. However, GPAs in the SWI/SNF complex in KRAS-mut ICB-treated NSCLCs were associated with poorer clinical outcomes. Patients with ARID1A/ARID1B/ARID2/PBRM1 mutations had a significantly shorter PFS (2.7 vs. 6.5 m, HR = 2.44 [95% CI 1.31–4.54], P = 0.004) than did those with SWI/SNF-wt. Among STK11wtKEAP1wtKRASmut NSCLCs, all SWI/SNF-mut (4.9 vs. 9.1 m, HR = 2.03 [95% CI 1.07–3.86], P = 0.029) and ARID1A/ARID1B/ARID2/PBRM1-mut (3.2 vs. 9.1 m, HR = 2.68 [95% CI 1.33–5.41], P = 0.004) NSCLCs had significantly shortened PFS, and ARID1A/ARID1B/ARID2-mut NSCLCs also tended to have a shorter overall survival (OS) (12.2 vs. 29.9 m, HR = 2.20 [95% CI 0.98–4.91], P = 0.052). Furthermore, RNA-seq and Western blot analyses confirmed that the deletion of SWI/SNF genes resulted in downregulated STING expression in NSCLC cell lines. And IHC analysis of patient tumour samples confirmed that the loss of SWI/SNF protein expression was associated with decreased STING protein levels. Notably, downregulated STING protein expression was observed in KRAS-mut NSCLC patients who did not benefit from ICB treatment.
Conclusions
In KRAS-mut NSCLCs with or without STK11/KEAP1 mutations, the GPAs in the DNA-binding genes ARID1A/ARID2 affected the outcomes of immunotherapy, possibly through the downregulation of STING expression.

Keywords: Non-small cell lung cancer, SWI/SNF, KRAS, Immunotherapy
Background
Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related death both worldwide and in China [1]. Among all lung cancer cases, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the main pathological type, accounting for 85.0% [2]. Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) has been the standard of care for advanced lung cancer. However, only a fraction of patients benefit from immunotherapy in the clinic. In patients with driver gene mutations, there are diverse results from ICB treatment, as those with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) rearrangements usually do not benefit from programmed death-1/programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-1/PD-L1) inhibition, and those with Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homologue (KRAS) mutations might benefit from compound gene mutations [3, 4]. KRAS-mut lung cancers are a group of heterogeneous diseases accounting for approximately 10% of Chinese and 30% of Caucasian lung cancers. The fact that not all KRAS-mut patients can benefit from ICB prompted an investigation of biomarkers associated with clinical outcomes.
More than 20% of human tumour, including lung cancer, have genomic alterations (GAs) in switch/sucrose nonfermentable (SWI/SNF) complex genes [5]. The SWI/SNF complex, also called the BRG1/BRM-associated factor (BAF) complex, functions in epigenetic regulation by altering the accessibility of chromatin [6]; it is involved in various biological processes, such as cell growth, cell division, cell proliferation, DNA damage repair (DDR), DNA replication and transcription [7]. There are three subfamilies of the SWI/SNF or BAF complex: canonical BRG1/BRM-associated factor (cBAF), polybromo-associated BAF (PBAF) and noncanonical BAF (ncBAF) [6], all of which are composed of diverse subunits. SMARCD, SMARCB1 and SMARCC are the main scaffolds, and SMARCA2 (BRM) and SMARCA4 (BRG1) make up the ATPases. ARID1A and ARID1B are unique subunits of cBAF; PBRM1 and ARID2 are unique to PBAF; and GLTSCR1 and BRD9 are unique to ncBAF. ARID1A, ARID1B and ARID2 are members of the AT-rich interaction domain (ARID) family, and they can specifically bind AT-rich DNA sequences at the beta-globin locus [8]. Mutations in the subunits are mainly classified as loss of function (LOF), which includes nonsense, deletion/insertion, frameshift and copy number loss mutations. However, missense mutations, especially those occurring at low frequencies, are still difficult to interpret [9–11].
The effects of the SWI/SNF complex on the outcomes of ICB could be subunit-specific and/or context specific. In KRAS-mut NSCLC patients treated with ICB, genomic pathogenic alterations (GPAs) in SWI/SNF subunits have been reported to have controversial effects on clinical outcomes [12]. In addition, mutations in STK11 and KEAP1 potentially compromise the ICB response and are frequently coaltered with GAs in SWI/SNF subunits [13]. Thus, GPAs in the SWI/SNF complex are heterogeneous and still controversial in association with the ICB treatment response in and clinical outcome of patients with NSCLC. In this study, we assessed the GPAs in the BAF complex in ICB-treated KRAS-mut NSCLC patients. We also explored the dysregulated gene expression potentially related to the ICB response in SWI/SNF-altered lung cancers, aiming to discover additional predictive or prognostic biomarkers for the specific setting of KRAS-mut lung cancers.
Methods
Patients
A cohort of patients treated at Guangdong Provincial People’s Hospital (GDPH) was included in this study. The cohort included 2660 NSCLC patients who underwent next-generation sequencing (NGS) from June 2016 through March 2022. Among the 2660 patients analysed, 787 (29.6%) underwent plasma NGS, 728 (27.4%) underwent tissue NGS and 1145 patients (43.0%) were tested for both tissue NGS and plasma NGS. Patients with pathogenic mutations in exons 18–21 of the EGFR gene and ALK-EML4 fusions based on NGS test results were excluded. Among the 2660 patients evaluated in the overall cohort, 299 patients received ICB therapy (anti-PD-1/PD-L1 therapy or anti-PD-1/PD-L1 plus chemotherapy) for advanced disease (Fig. 1). Information on variables, including age, sex, smoking status, histologic type, mutation status, PD-L1 status, tumour mutational burden (TMB), and line and type of ICB, was collected for analysis. The last follow-up date was June 2022, and patients without an endpoint were censored. We calculated overall survival (OS) from the date of diagnosis to the date of death for any reason. Progression-free survival (PFS) was measured from the start of immunotherapy until the date of death or disease progression. Informed consent was obtained from each patient, and this study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of GDPH.
DNA extraction and next-generation sequencing (NGS)
Prior to immunotherapy administration, tissue samples from patients who received ICB therapy were analysed via NGS. Tissue DNA was extracted from formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumour tissues using a QIAamp DNA FFPE Tissue Kit, and circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) was extracted from 4–5 ml of each plasma sample using a QIAamp Circulating Nucleic Acid Kit (Qiagen). Fragments between 200 and 400 bp from the sheared tissue DNA and cfDNA were purified (Agencourt AMPure XP Kit, Beckman Coulter), hybridized with capture probe baits, selected with magnetic beads, and amplified. Target capture was performed using a commercial panel consisting of 520 genes (OncoScreen Plus) spanning 1.64 megabases of the human genome. The quality and size of the fragments were assessed using a high-sensitivity DNA kit and a Bioanalyzer 2100 (Agilent Technologies). Indexed samples were sequenced on a NextSeq 500 (Illumina) with paired-end reads and an average sequencing depth of 2000 × for tissue samples and 10,000 × for liquid biopsy samples. Sequence data were mapped to the reference human genome (hg19) via Burrows–Wheeler Aligner version 0.7.10 [14]. Local alignment optimization, duplication marking and variant calling were performed using Genome Analysis Tool Kit version 3.2 [15] and VarScan version 2.4.3 [16]. The samples were compared against their own white blood cell controls to identify somatic variants. Variants were filtered using the VarScan fpfilter pipeline, and loci with depths less than 100 were filtered out. Base calling in plasma and tissue samples required at least 8 supporting reads for single-nucleotide variations (SNVs) and 2 and 5 supporting reads for insertion‒deletion variations (Indels), respectively. Variants with a population frequency greater than 0.1% in the ExAC, 1000 Genomes, dbSNP or ESP6500SI-V2 databases were grouped as single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and excluded from further analysis. The remaining variants were annotated with ANNOVAR (2016–02-01 release) [17] and SnpEff version 3.6 [18]. Analyses of structural variations (SVs) were performed using Factera version 1.4.3 [19]. Copy number variations (CNVs) were analysed on the basis of the depth of coverage data of capture intervals. Coverage data were corrected for sequencing bias resulting from the GC content and probe design. The average coverage of all captured regions was used to normalize the coverage of different samples to comparable scales. The copy number was calculated on the basis of the ratio between the depth of coverage in tumour samples and the average coverage of an adequate number (n > 50) of samples without CNVs as references per capture interval. CNV is called if the coverage data of the gene region are quantitatively and statistically significant from its reference control. The limit of detection for CNVs was 1.5 for copy number deletions and 2.64 for copy number amplifications.
Assessment of genomic pathogenic alterations (GPAs) in lung cancer genes and SWI/SNF subunits
Patients with pathogenic mutations in EGFR exons 18, 19, 20 and 21 and ALK-EML4 fusion mutations were excluded. We analysed the SWI/SNF genes most commonly found in NSCLC: ARID1A, ARID1B, ARID2, PBRM1, SMARCA4, SMARCA2, SMARCB1, SMARCD1 and SMARCE1. According to OncoKB, all loss-of-function alterations in these SWI/SNF complex genes were classified as deleterious mutations, and all oncogenic alterations (deletion, truncating mutations, insertion, nonsense, missense mutations) in the KRAS, STK11, KEAP1, TP53 and SWI/SNF complex genes were classified as deleterious mutations [12]. To determine the pathogenicity of mutations not annotated in OncoKB, we first searched the Catalog of Somatic Mutations in Cancer (COSMIC) database for the identified missense mutations. Then, Polymorphism Phenotyping v2 (PolyPhen-2) was used to evaluate the functional significance of each missense mutation. A deleterious missense mutation was defined as both a pathogenic mutation reported by COSMIC and a Polyphen2 score greater than 0.909 (probably damaging). The term “SWI/SNF mutant” referred to patients harbouring one or more deleterious SWI/SNF gene mutations. In the naming of subgroups with two or more subunits, the presence of any subunit mutation was defined as “mut”. The “SWI/SNF-wt” group was defined as having no mutations in SWI/SNF subunits. To explore the effects of different BAF complexes and ARID genes on survival, we further subdivided patients with SWI/SNF mutations into the following groups: ARID1A/ARID1B mut, PBRM1/ARID2 mut, ARID(1A/1B/2)/PBRM1 mut and ARID(1A/1B/2) mut (ARID1A and ARID1B are the unique subunits of cBAF; PBRM1 and ARID2 are unique for PBAF; and ARID1A, ARID1B and ARID2 are the members of the AT-rich interaction domain (ARID) family).
TMB and PD-L1 assessment
TMB was computed as the ratio between the number of nonsynonymous mutations detected and the sequence length of the panel. The mutation count included nonsynonymous SNVs and Indels and excluded hot mutation events, CNVs, SVs and germline SNPs. Only mutations with an allelic fraction (AF) of ≥ 2% for tissue samples and ≥ 0.2% for plasma samples were included in the mutation count. For accurate TMB calculations, the maximum AF (maxAF) was ≥ 5% for tissue and ≥ 1% for plasma. The total size of the sequencing region for estimating TMB was 1.003 Mb.
Immunohistochemistry was performed using the 22C3 (Dako, Dako platform) antibody to determine the PD-L1 tumour proportion score (TPS).
Whole-exome sequencing (WES) analysis
Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was performed as previously described [20]. A TIANamp Genomic DNA Kit (Tiangen Biotech, DP304) was used to extract DNA. Then, the DNA was fragmented, purified and size-selected (100–250 bp). A customized capture probe (length, 53 M; Integrated DNA Technologies) was used to construct libraries from at least 10 ng of DNA. Next, DNA libraries (20 ng/μL) were sequenced. The captured libraries were paired-end and then sequenced with Geneplus-2000 in lengths of 2100 bp. The raw data were filtered using fastp (version 1). Among the samples, only those with high-quality reads (Phred scores > 30) were retained for further analysis. Burrows‒Wheeler alignment (BWA version 0.7.10) was then used to map the clean reads to the reference human genome (hg19). We then removed duplicate reads and realigned local indels using GATK (version 4.0). All software tools were run with default parameters.
Immunohistochemistry (IHC)
All formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) samples were sectioned (5 µm thick) for haematoxylin‒eosin (H&E) staining and IHC. The sections were incubated in an oven at 60 °C for 2 h. Dewaxed sections were repaired with IHC antigen repair solution (GTR, GT100411) at 120 °C for 3 min, cooled and incubated in 3.0% H2O2 for 10 min to eliminate endogenous enzymes. The sections were soaked in PBS 3 times for 5 min each and then blocked with 5.0% BSA (Solarbio) solution for 1 h at room temperature. After soaking in PBS 3 times for 5 min each, the sections were incubated with antibodies against SMARCA4 (Abcam, ab110641, 1:200), ARID1A (CST, 12,354, 1:500), APOBEC3B (Proteintech, 14,559–1-AP, 1:200), ADAMTS12 (Proteintech, 24,934–1-AP, 1:200), ICAM1 (CST, 67,836, 1:200) and STING (CST, 13,647, 1:50/1:100) at room temperature for 1 h. The sections were immersed in PBS 3 times for 5 min each and then incubated with a secondary antibody using an IHC secondary antibody kit (Absin, abs996) at room temperature for 30 min. The sections were washed again with PBS 3 times for 5 min each, and colour was developed with a DAB chromogenic kit (Coolaber). The sections were counterstained with haematoxylin (Sigma), rinsed in tap water for 20 min, dried naturally, immersed in xylene for 5 min and sealed with neutral resin.
The staining results were interpreted by two independent pathologists blinded to the clinicopathological data. The H score [21] was used for semiquantitative analyses of the staining intensity and percentage of stained tumour tissue sections.
Cell cultures
The human lung cancer cell lines NCI-H23, NCI-H441, NCI-H460, NCI-H520, NCI-H1299, NCI-H1581 and A549 were used and confirmed by short tandem repeat (STR) tests before experiments. A Takara Mycoplasma assay kit (Takara, CY232) was used to ensure that the cell line was free of mycoplasma contamination. The cells were cultured in RPMI 1640 basic (1 ×) medium (Gibco) containing 10% foetal bovine serum (Gibco, 1932594 C) in a sterile cell incubator at 37 °C and 5.0% CO2.
Western blot analysis
Ice-cold PBS was used to wash the cells in a 10-cm dish twice. RIPA buffer (APExBlO, K1020-100) was used to extract protein by lysis for 30 min on ice. The lysates were centrifuged for 15 min at 4 °C at 13,500 × g, and the supernatant was retained. A bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay (Solarbio) was used to determine the protein concentration, and an SDS‒PAGE gel (Vazyme, E301‒01) was used to separate the proteins. The proteins were transferred to PVDF membranes (Thermo Scientific™, 88,518), which were then washed with TBST (Absin, abs952-1 L). The membranes were incubated in blocking solution containing 5% skim milk (Solarbio, D8340) in TBST for 1 h at room temperature, followed by an overnight incubation with a primary antibody (anti-ARID1A, 1:1000, CST, 12354S; anti-ARID1B, 1:1000, CST, 92,964; anti-SMARCA4, 1:10,000, Abcam, ab110641; anti-SMARCA2, 1:1000, CST, 11,966; anti-ARID2, 1:1000, CST, 82,342; anti-PBRM1, 1:1000, CST, 38,439; anti-Vinculin, 1:1000, CST, 13901S; anti-APOBEC3B, 1:500, Proteintech, 14,559–1-AP; and anti-STING, 1:100, CST, 13,647) at 4 °C. After the membranes were washed three times with TBST, they were incubated with a horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibody (anti-rabbit IgG, 1:2000, CST, 7074) at room temperature for 60 min. Clarity Max Western ECL Substrate (Bio-Rad, 1,705,062) was used to visualize the protein bands. ImageJ was used to calculate and analyse the grey values of the bands.
RNA extraction and sequencing (RNA-seq)
Total RNA was isolated using an Animal Total RNA Extraction Kit (Magnetic Bead Method T102096). A TruSeq® RNA Sample Preparation Kit (Illumina) was used to prepare paired-end libraries. We used poly-T magnetic beads to purify the poly-A-containing mRNA molecules. As soon as the mRNA was purified, fragmentation was carried out using divalent cations at 94 °C for 8 min. Reverse transcription was performed with random primers to generate first-strand cDNA from the cleaved RNA. RNase H and DNA Polymerase I were then used for second-strand cDNA synthesis. Then, the fragments were subjected to end repair, the addition of one ‘A’ base, and finally adapter ligation. A cDNA library was created after purifying the products and amplifying them via PCR. A Qubit® 2.0 fluorometer (Life Technologies) and Agilent 2100 bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies) were used to quantify and validate the purified libraries. After cluster generation by cBot with a diluted library, sequences were performed on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000. Shanghai Biotechnology Corporation constructed and sequenced the library.
Quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT‒PCR)
A cDNA reverse transcription kit (Vazyme, R323-01) was used to perform reverse transcription in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. The concentration of cDNA was subsequently normalized with nuclease-free water. SYBR Green qPCR Master Mix (Esscience, QP002) was used for qPCR, and GAPDH was used as an internal positive control. Next, we performed qRT‒PCR for ARID1A, ARID1B, ARID2, PBRM1, SMARCA4, SMARCA2, APOBEC3B, ADAMTS12 and STING.
Data analysis for gene expression
Raw reads were preprocessed by filtering out rRNA reads, sequencing adapters, short-fragment reads and other low-quality reads. We used HISAT2 (version 2.0.4) to map the clean reads to the GRCh38 reference genome with two mismatches. After genome mapping, Stringtie (version: 1.3.0) was run with a reference annotation to generate FPKM values for known gene models. Differential gene expression analysis was performed using edgeR [22]. Nonexpressed genes (< 1 FPKM expression in all samples) were filtered out. False discovery rates (FDRs) were used as thresholds for P value significance in multiple tests. Differentially expressed genes were selected according to an FDR ≤ 0.05 and a fold change ≥ 2. Three replicates were used for each cell line.
Statistical analysis
The chi-square test and Fisher’s exact test were used to compare the distributions of categorical factors, and Student’s t test was used to compare continuous variables. The log-rank test was used to compare survival estimated by Kaplan‒Meier curves. Univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards models were used to analyse variables associated with survival, and a multivariate model was constructed using associated variables with P < 0.1 in univariate analysis. The Mann‒Whitney U test was used to compare the TMB, PD-L1 expression and H-score. Statistical analyses were conducted using R, RStudio, GraphPad Prism and IBM SPSS Statistics. All P values are deemed significant at less than 0.05 on a two-sided basis.
Results
Baseline patient characteristics and SWI/SNF GPAs in advanced NSCLC patients receiving ICB therapy
A total of 2660 NSCLC patients underwent NGS. Deleterious mutations in SWI/SNF complex genes were observed in 401 patients (15.0%) (Fig. 2A). SMARCA4 was mutated in 31.4% of the patients, ARID1A in 25.9%, ARID2 in 10.0%, PBRM1 in 9.2%, ARID1B in 7.5%, SMARCB1 in 1.5%, and SMARCD1 in 0.7%; there was > 1 SWI/SNF gene alteration in 13.7% of the patients (Fig. 2B). Among the 401 patients who had deleterious SWI/SWF mutations, the most frequently coaltered lung cancer genes were TP53 (73.3%), EGFR (29.7%), KRAS (22.9%), KEAP1 (20.2%), STK11 (13.2%), MET (12.0%), ALK-EML4 fusion (3.5%), BRAF V600E (1.5%), RET-CD74 fusion (1.5%) and ROS1-CD74 fusion (0.5%). Figure 2C shows the full spectrum of the deleterious mutations of these genes.
After excluding patients with clinically actionable alterations in EGFR and ALK, 299 patients with advanced NSCLC treated with ICB therapy were included (Table 1). Two hundred and thirty patients (76.9%) had tumour with wild-type SWI/SNF, and 69 patients (23.1%) had GPAs in SWI/SNF. The genomic status of the SWI/SNF complex was not significantly different on the basis of age, ECOG PS, smoking history, histologic type, brain metastasis, frequency of KRAS mutation or PD-L1 TPS. The majority of the patients (233/299, 77.9%) were males; the median age of the cohort was 61 years (range 14–81); and in males, the rate of SWI/SNF mutations was greater (P = 0.004). A total of 69.6% (208/299) of the tumour were advanced adenocarcinomas at presentation, and 59.9% (179/299) of the patients were smokers. Moreover, we observed a greater TMB (P < 0.001) in SWI/SNF-mutant NSCLC patients than in SWI/SNF-wt NSCLC patients.

Outcomes of ICB therapy in all NSCLC patients
Among the 299 patients with advanced NSCLCs receiving ICB therapy, there were no significant differences in ICB therapy efficacy between the SWI/SNF-wt and SWI/SNF-mut patients in terms of the overall response rate (ORR) (27.7% vs. 24.1%, P = 0.67, Additional file 1: Fig. S2A), PFS (5.5 vs. 5.5 m, HR = 0.97 [95% CI 0.72–1.33], P = 0.860, Additional file 1: Fig. S2B) and OS (27.5 vs. 22.5 m, HR = 1.13 [95% CI 0.80–1.60], P = 0.480, Additional file 1: Fig. S2C). We next analysed the effects of mutations in the subunits of the SWI/SNF complex, including SMARCA4, ARID1A, ARID1A/ARID1B and PBRM1/ARID2, on the response to ICB therapy. Survival analysis revealed that mutations in SMARCA4, ARID1A, ARID1A/ARID1B and PBRM1/ARID2 had no significant effects on the ORR, PFS or OS of patients with advanced NSCLC receiving ICB therapy (Additional file 1: Fig. S3).
The variables that were associated with outcomes of ICB therapy (defined as P < 0.1 for either PFS or OS) in the univariate analysis (Additional file 2: Table. S1), such as age, sex, line of ICB therapy, TMB and mutation state of KRAS, STK11 and KEAP1, were included in a multivariate model (Additional file 2: Table. S2).
Effects of SWI/SNF GPAs on ICB therapy outcomes in patients with KRAS-mut NSCLC
Among the 90 patients with KRAS-mut advanced NSCLC, 25 (27.8%) had deleterious mutations in the SWI/SNF complex (Additional file 2: Table. S3 and Additional file 1: Fig. S4A). The genomic status of the SWI/SNF complex was not significantly different on the basis of age, sex, smoking history, histologic type, frequency of STK11 and KEAP1 mutations or PD-L1 TPS. We also observed a greater TMB (P = 0.016) in SWI/SNF-mutant NSCLC patients than in SWI/SNF-wt NSCLC patients. For the 25 patients with SWI/SNF-mut and KRAS-mut tumours, the frequency of GPAs in each SWI/SNF gene is shown in Additional file 1: Fig. S4B. The most frequently coaltered genes were TP53 (56.0%), STK11 (28.0%) and KEAP1 (20.0%) (Additional file 1: Fig. S4C).

Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in cancer cells with SWI/SNF GPAs
To investigate the possible molecular mechanism by which SWI/SNF gene mutations affect ICB therapy efficacy in advanced NSCLC patients, we selected seven NSCLC cell lines (NCI-H23, NCI-H441, NCI-H460, NCI-H520, NCI-H1299, NCI-H1581 and A549) that do not have EGFR and ALK pathogenic mutations on the basis of whole exome sequencing (WES) results. The most frequently mutated gene was TP53 (7/7; 100.0%), followed by KRAS (4/7; 57.0%). SMARCA4 was the most frequently mutated SWI/SNF gene (3/7; 43.0%), followed by SMARCA2, ARID1A and ARID2 (2/7; 29.0%), and ARID1B (1/7; 14.0%). No mutations in PBRM1 were detected in any of the 7 cell lines (Additional file 1: Fig. S10A). Then, we performed Western blot (WB) analysis to verify the expression of the SWI/SNF protein (Fig. 5A-B) and qPCR to verify the expression of SWI/SNF mRNA (Fig. 5C).
The cells were divided into four groups on the basis of the presence of KRAS and SWI/SNF mutations. The KRAS-mut group included H23, A549, H460 and H441 cells, and the KRAS-wt group (pan-negative group, PN) included H1581, H520 and H1299 cells. SWI/SNF mutations were found in three cell lines (H23, A549 and H460) in the KRAS-mut group and in two cell lines (H1581 and H520) in the PN group. To gain further insight into the transcriptomic changes underlying the phenotypic alterations associated with SWI/SNF mutations, we compared the gene expression profiles of SWI/SNF-wt and SWI/SNF-mut cells using RNA-seq. In the KRAS-mut group, 2800 genes were upregulated and 1766 genes were downregulated in the SWI/SNF-mut group as compared with the SWI/SNF-wt group, whereas in the PN group, 2476 genes were upregulated and 1131 genes were downregulated (Additional file 1: Fig. S10B).
Intrinsic innate immune activity within tumour cells influences the response to ICB therapy [23]. Thus, we focused our attention on genes involved in the regulation of immune activity. A selected list of genes associated with immune pathways from the GO database (http://geneontology.org/) was intersected with the differentially expressed genes identified in our study. Eighty-nine significantly dysregulated genes were identified (Additional file 1: Fig. S10C), and their expression in SWI/SNF-mut and SWI/SNF-wt cells is shown in Fig. 5D. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed that the CD8+ T cell response pathway was suppressed in the SWI/SNF-mut group, with STING and APOBEC3B identified as core genes (Fig. 5E). STING is a key regulatory gene related to tumour innate immunity [24, 25]. APOBEC3B is also associated with the expression of immune genes and plays a crucial role in predicting the immunotherapy response in patients with breast cancer and NSCLC [26–29].
We subsequently analysed the protein expression levels of APOBEC3B and STING in the cell lines. Initial validation was conducted using WB and qPCR analyses of the dysregulated molecules associated with SWI/SNF genes. We found that STING protein expression was significantly lower in the SWI/SNF-mut group than in the SWI/SNF-wt group (P < 0.05; Fig. 5F,G). Similarly, STING mRNA expression was lower in the SWI/SNF-mut group than in the SWI/SNF-wt group (P < 0.05; Fig. 5H). The expression level of the APOBEC3B protein in SWI/SNF-mut cells (H460 and H1581) was greater than that in SWI/SNF-wt cells (H441 and H1299) (Fig. 5F,G). Additionally, the expression level of APOBEC3B mRNA in SWI/SNF-mut cells (A549, H23 and H520) was greater than that in SWI/SNF-wt cells (H441 and H1299) (Fig. 5H).
Dysregulated STING and APOBEC3B in clinical SWI/SNF-mut tumours in relation to ICB therapy outcome
To explore and validate the effects of SWI/SNF GPAs on the protein expression levels of four differentially expressed genes in NSCLC patients, as well as the underlying mechanism for the significantly reduced efficacy of ICB therapy in advanced KRAS and SWI/SNF mutant NSCLC patients, we evaluated the expression of ARID1A, SMARCA4, APOBEC3B and STING using IHC and samples from 37 advanced NSCLC patients. On the basis of the NGS results, the 37 patients were divided into the SWI/SNF-mut group (n = 6) and the SWI/SNF-wt group (n = 31). The expression levels of ARID1A (median H score: 7.50 vs. 80.0, P = 0.030) and SMARCA4 (median H score: 5.0 vs. 87.5, P = 0.025) in SWI/SNF-mut patients were significantly lower than those in SWI/SNF-wt patients (Fig. 6A).
Notably, the protein expression level of APOBEC3B in SWI/SNF-mut patients was significantly greater than that in SWI/SNF-wt patients (median H-score: 95.0 vs. 7.5, P = 0.004). Additionally, compared with SWI/SNF-wt patients, SWI/SNF-mut patients presented significantly lower STING (median H score: 2.5 vs. 30.0, P = 0.020) expression (Fig. 6B).
Additionally, patients with low expression of SWI/SNF proteins (ARID1A and SMARCA4) had a mPFS of 5.9 months, numerically lower than the 6.8 months in those with high expression (P = 0.40, Additional file 1: Fig. S11A), the mPFS in the ARID1A proteins low expression group was also numerically lower than those in the ARID1A proteins high expression group, but the differences were not statistically significant (4.8 vs 8.1, P = 0.10) (Additional file 1: Fig. S11B). And there were no statistically significant PFS differences between low and high SMARCA4 expression (6.8 vs 6.9, P = 0.53, Additional file 1: Fig. S11C), STING expression (5.9 vs 6.8, P = 0.87, Additional file 1: Fig. S11D) and APOBEC3B expression (5.9 vs 7.2, P = 0.32, Additional file 1: Fig. S11E). Prior to and after immunotherapy, CT imaging was performed on patients. Figure 6C shows representative pretreatment and posttreatment CT images of SWI/SNF-mut and SWI/SNF-wt patients treated with ICB. The left image shows that the tumour lesion of a SWI/SNF-wt patient whose PFS was 30.6 months significantly decreased after 5 months of ICB treatment. Conversely, in an ARID1A-mut patient (right), a CT scan after 1 month of immunotherapy revealed tumour enlargement, and the PFS of this patient was 1.3 months.
Discussion
An FDA pooled analysis found that KRAS-mutant NSCLCs receiving first-line ICB plus chemotherapy may have better OS than KRAS wild-type patients [30]. However, KRAS-mut lung cancers represent a heterogeneous group, some KRAS-mut patients with co-alterations of STK11/KEAP1 could not benefit much from immunotherapy [31]. In addition to KRAS genotypes and compound mutations in STK11, TP53, and cell cycle genes, other molecular biomarkers warrant further exploration to identify patients who may benefit from ICB. In this study, we investigated the effects of SWI/SNF GPAs in patients with KRAS-mut lung cancer treated with ICB and the potential mechanism mediating the response to ICB. Among the 299 NSCLC patients, SWI/SNF genes were found to be mutated in 23.0% of the entire cohort and in 28.0% (25/90) of patients with advanced KRAS-mut lung cancer. Consistent with previous studies [12, 13, 32–34], we also found that SWI/SNF gene mutations were more common in smokers, males, and patients with a higher TMB. The most frequently comutated genes were KEAP1 and STK11. SMARCA4 presented the highest mutation rate, at 38.0%, followed by ARID1A, at 24.0%, among the 299 NSCLC patients.
The GPAs in SWI/SWF did not seem to affect immunotherapy efficacy among the general NSCLC population of 299 patients, who were selected from 2660 patients by excluding patients with EGFR/ALK alterations and other disease stages or histological reasons. We subsequently analysed the effects of SWI/SWF alterations on clinical outcomes in KRAS-mut NSCLC patients treated with ICB, as outcomes among such patients are still debated [12, 35, 36]. Compared with wild-type SWI/SWF, SWI/SWF alterations seem to confer worse immunotherapy outcomes for KRAS-mut patients. A significantly shorter PFS in patients with SWI/SNF GPAs was observed. Alterations in ARID1A (unique to cBAF) and ARID2 (unique to PBAF) are the main factors associated with poor immunotherapy efficacy in KRAS-mut NSCLC patients. ARID1A, ARID1B and ARID2 are members of the ARID family and encode AT-rich DNA interacting domain-containing proteins. These findings suggest that the DNA-binding components of the SWI/SNF complex functionally mediate the adverse effects of immunotherapy. Notably, the detrimental effects of SWI/SNF GPAs on immunotherapy persisted even after patients with mutations in STK11 and KEAP1 were excluded.
To determine the significance of SWI/SNF gene alterations, a key point is to precisely define the deleterious LOF mutations among all SWI/SNF alterations. In this study, LOF GAs were defined as nonsense, frame-shift insertions or deletions, splice-site variants, homozygous deletions and pathogenic missense mutations [34, 37, 38]. All LOF mutations and pathogenic missense mutations in SWI/SNF genes were retained for further analysis. This study seeks to comprehensively analyse ARID1A and ARID2 alterations in Chinese KRAS-mut NSCLCs receiving ICB, demonstrating their independent prognostic value beyond STK11/KEAP1 co-mutations. The presence of mutations in ARID1A and ARID2 is associated with worse PFS in Chinese STK11wtKEAP1wtKRASmut NSCLCs undergoing immunotherapy.
Several previous studies have reported that the aforementioned gene mutations in advanced NSCLC patients are associated with a poor prognosis in relation to immunotherapy [39–43]. Furthermore, patients with other types of cancer who were ARID1A negative were shown to experience shorter cancer-specific survival, according to multivariate survival analyses [44–50]. Other studies have reported that in NSCLC patients treated with PD-1/PD-L1/CTLA-4 inhibitors, mutations in ARID1A/ARID2 of the SWI/SNF complex are correlated with better outcomes than those in wild-type ARID1A/ARID2. However, none of the aforementioned studies excluded the effect of lung cancer driver gene mutations on immunotherapy outcomes in patients [51–54]. A study by the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute suggested that SMARCA4 mutations may lead to poorer immunotherapy outcomes in patients with KRAS-mutant NSCLC [12]. PBRM1 mutations are also associated with significantly longer PFS in patients with NSCLC receiving immunotherapy [55, 56]. Overall, ARID1A and ARID2 are intriguing biomarkers for outcomes after immunotherapy in NSCLC patients, warranting further extensive investigation. On the basis of the results of our study, the most common SWI/SNF mutations in KRAS-mut NSCLC are detrimental to immunotherapy efficacy.
Mutations in STK11 and KEAP1 have been associated with poor clinical outcomes among KRAS-mut NSCLC patients receiving chemotherapy and immunotherapy [31, 57–59]. To clarify the potential confounding roles of these two genes, we reanalysed the data after excluding patients with STK11 and KEAP1 mutations. The detrimental effects of ARID1A and ARID2 mutations on the outcomes of immunotherapy in patients with KRAS-mut NSCLC remained. Our study identified ARID1A/ARID2 as the primary contributors to poor outcomes in Chinese KRAS-mut NSCLCs, due to the limited sample size for ARID1B-mut (n = 1) and PBRM1-mut (n = 1) cases. Future studies with larger sample sizes are needed to validate the role of these less frequent mutations.
To explore the potential molecular mechanisms by which SWI/SNF GPAs have deleterious effects on immunotherapy in KRAS-mut NSCLC patients, we sequenced lung cancer cell lines using WES in combination with RNA-seq. Differential expression analysis revealed that the expression of STING was downregulated whereas that of APOBEC3B was upregulated in NSCLC cells harbouring SWI/SNF GPAs. We subsequently assessed the protein levels of these targets by IHC using clinical samples. Downregulated STING expression and upregulated APOBEC3B expression at the protein level were confirmed in tumours containing SWI/SNF GPAs.
Apolipoprotein B mRNA editing enzyme catalytic subunit 3B (APOBEC3B), a member of the APOBEC family, plays a critical role in both innate and adaptive immune responses [60] as well as in cancer development and progression. The expression of APOBEC3B in NSCLC is associated with intertumoural heterogeneity [61–63] and poor outcomes in patients with lung cancer [64], as confirmed in the TCGA database of patients with NSCLC [26]. The role of APOBEC3B overexpression in ICB resistance in NSCLC remains largely unknown and warrants further investigation.
Notably, STING expression was downregulated in cell lines and clinical samples with SWI/SNF GPAs. Low levels of STING were also correlated with inferior outcomes of ICB treatment. STING is a key node in the cGAS‐STING pathway, transducing signals for immunity, and is recognized as a potent regulator of the tumour immune microenvironment during cancer progression [65–69]. During anticancer immunity, cancer cell-intrinsic immunity pathways, such as the cGAS-STING signalling pathway, can produce cytokines through the accumulation of cytosolic DNA/RNA in cancer cells. When cancer cells are devoid of intrinsic cGAS-STING signalling, T cell infiltration and the response to checkpoint blockade are reduced [70, 71]. In a variety of cancers, cGAS-STING signalling is suppressed, and the downregulation of cancer cell-intrinsic cGAS-STING expression is associated with poor prognosis [72–76]. Researchers have shown that reactivating LKB1 or the STING pathway may enhance anticancer immunity in NSCLC that is resistant to immune checkpoint blockade [77]. Additionally, the activation of cGAS-STING signalling promotes NK cell infiltration and antitumour immunity in NSCLC in vivo [78]. Those findings may explain why downregulated STING expression in SWI/SNF GPAs could be attributable to inferior ICB treatment outcomes in patients with KRAS-mutant NSCLC. However, how STING is regulated by SWI/SNF GPAs requires further investigation.
Our study has several limitations. This cohort of ICB-treated NSCLC patients was derived from a single academic cancer center and analysed retrospectively. The results need to be validated using a larger sample size. The NGS assay did not include SMARCA2, which is also an important SWI/SNF gene. Other research has linked SMARCA4 mutations in KRAS-mut NSCLC patients to less favourable outcomes of immunotherapy [12]. But in our study, the mOS (10.1 vs 21.6, P = 0.71) and mPFS (6.7 vs 6.5, P = 0.76) in the SMARCA4-mut subgroup were not significantly different as compared to the SMARCA4-wt subgroup among KRAS-mut NSCLC patients. It may be necessary to conduct a larger study to investigate the relationship between SMARCA4 and immunotherapy in patients with KRAS-mut NSCLC. Finally, the presence of mutations in SWI/SNF complex genes is common in NSCLC, but their distribution may vary among different populations. The mutation rate of SWI/SNF complex genes in European and American NSCLC patients is 20–30% [12, 51], whereas it is approximately 15% in the Chinese population [79], which aligns with our findings of 15%. Our study revealed that SMARCA4 has a mutation rate of 5%, ARID1A has 4%, and other genes have approximately 1% or less. Awad et al. reported the following frequencies for SWI/SNF gene alterations: ARID1A (5.8%), SMARCA4 (5.7%), ARID2 (3.2%) and ARID1B (1.7%); additionally, they reported that KRAS-mut NSCLC with SMARCA4 mutations may lead to poorer immunotherapy outcomes than NSCLC with wild-type SMARCA4 [12, 80]. Our investigation demonstrated that, in NSCLC patients with KRAS mutations, ARID family gene mutations are linked to shorter PFS following immunotherapy but that mutations in the SMARCA4 gene had no significant effect on immunotherapy efficacy.
Conclusions
In summary, SWI/SNF GPAs could serve as novel negative biomarkers to guide immunotherapy in KRAS-mutant NSCLC patients among the Chinese population, with a primary focus on GPAs in ARID1A and ARID2. The poor immunotherapy outcomes in KRAS-mut NSCLC patients harbouring SWI/SNF GPAs may be attributed to the dysregulated expression levels of APOBEC3B and STING. The independent validation of these findings requires additional prospective studies with larger sample sizes. Further studies exploring the mechanistic relationship of SWI/SNF (mainly ARID1A and ARID2) and with APOBEC3B and STING in KRAS-mut NSCLC are also warranted.
